method: Manual adversarial refutation, session 2026-07-25. Each candidate gets 1-3 targeted web searches attempting to find existing interdisciplinary work connecting the two fields. survived=false means prior art was found — the candidate is refuted, not a genuinely unasked question. This is the honest, non-automated version of upgrade (3) from the project pitch; see core/refuter.py for the upgrade path to an API-driven panel.

verdicts.reasoning: "Green and sustainable pharmacology" is a named interdisciplinary paradigm (Frontiers scoping review 2025) covering environmental impact of drug discovery/manufacturing, plus "ecopharmacovigilance" as an established subfield.

Dedicated 2025 arXiv roadmap for climate-relevant robotics research (energy, built environment, land use, Earth sciences), plus an active "ecorobotics"/environmental intelligence field with an Annual Reviews article.

"Immuno-inspired robotics" is an established subfield with review articles dating back to 2012 (arXiv), covering artificial-immune-system algorithms for robot navigation and multi-robot control, plus physical micro-robots built to probe immune cell function (U Chicago).

Mature, well-established connection: pharmacology cited as "one of the ten most frequently occurring disciplines in robotics research"; extensive literature on robotic drug discovery, dispensing, and pharmaceutical manufacturing automation.

"Natural Language Processing in Pharmacology" is an established field with its own review article in Pharmacological Reviews, covering drug-drug interaction extraction, psychoactive-drug-effect language analysis, and pharmaceutical-literature text mining.
verdicts.note: First candidate tested against the corrected abstract-text signal (not concept/topic tags) -- still refuted.

verdicts.reasoning: Socially assistive robots for depression/mental health, robotic transcranial magnetic stimulation for depression treatment, and robotic-assisted gait therapy effects on depression symptoms are all active, published research threads -- just not co-tagged under both concept IDs, which is why tag-based counting showed zero.
verdicts.note: Fine-grained topic-level test (OpenAlex topic 'Treatment of Major Depression' vs the robotics concept). Demonstrates concept/topic tag co-occurrence undercounts real connections.

verdicts.reasoning: "Self-driving labs" and AI-driven robotic chemists for autonomous organic synthesis are an active, named research area with multiple Nature-family papers -- again a tagging gap, not a real absence.
verdicts.note: Same tagging-undercount pattern as the depression case above; together these motivated switching the whole pipeline to abstract-text counting.

noise_findings.verdict: not a real candidate -- false signal, not refuted prior art
noise_findings.reasoning: The single co-occurring paper (OpenAlex W2753513162) is an unrelated ophthalmology-journal editorial summarizing many unrelated studies; it mentions both words in passing while describing different papers, not a paper about apelin and robotics together. Read via abstract_inverted_index before trusting the count. Lesson: any candidate with very low n_ab needs the actual connecting paper(s) read, not just counted -- sparse co-occurrence can itself be noise.

finding: 0/8 real candidates survived refutation across four distinct methodological attempts this session: (1) broad disciplines from a citation-sampled corpus, (2) broad disciplines from true global tag-based counts, (3) fine-grained pharmacology topics vs. robotics via tags, (4) broad disciplines via corrected abstract-text counts. Pattern: for any two moderately-broad, well-known academic fields, if a productive combination exists, someone has usually already published a review naming it -- academia actively hunts for and names interdisciplinary connections between recognizable fields (see sources above: 'ecorobotics', 'green pharmacology', 'immuno-inspired robotics', 'NLP in pharmacology' are all named subfields with their own reviews). This is not a bug fixable by better counting -- discipline-level and topic-level search keeps rediscovering gaps that already got filled. The genuinely unexplored territory, if it exists, requires finer granularity than anything tried here (OpenAlex has 252 subfields and 4,516 topics -- ~10.2M possible topic-level pairs), which is the actual argument for why the bandit matters: it's the only way to search that space without brute-forcing millions of API calls.
